etymology: Greek huakinthos (G5191/G5192) — a precious stone of deep blue or blue-violet color, identified today as a variety of zircon or sapphire; the eleventh foundation of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20). The same Greek word names the flower hyacinth.
biblical_def: Jacinth is the eleventh foundation stone of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20). The Greek huakinthos covers both a flower (hyacinth) and a deep blue-violet stone, probably modern zircon or sapphire. The same word appears in Revelation 9:17 describing the breastplates of the demonic horsemen of the sixth trumpet: "having breastplates of fire, and of jacinth, and brimstone" — fire (red), jacinth (deep blue), brimstone (sulfur-yellow) — the colors of judgment. Yet here in Revelation 21 the same color crowns the eleventh course of the city's eternal foundation. Eleven is sometimes the biblical number of incompleteness or transition (eleven faithful disciples after Judas fell, before Matthias was chosen, Acts 1:26; eleven days from Horeb to Kadesh-Barnea, Deut 1:2 — the journey Israel could have completed in eleven days but turned into forty years through unbelief). The eleventh foundation, jacinth, sits at the threshold of the city's completion — one stone shy of the twelfth and final stone. The blue-violet of jacinth pictures the deep of heaven; the city's penultimate foundation reaches into that blue. In the high priestly garments the blue of the ephod and the blue of the lace fastening the breastplate to the ephod (Exod 28:28, 31, 37) recurs throughout — blue is the priestly color of heavenly origin. Jacinth gathers up that thread into the foundation of the city where every priest-believer reigns with Christ.
webster_summary: A deep blue-violet precious stone; the eleventh foundation of the New Jerusalem.
webster_full: JACINTH, noun. A precious stone of a deep blue or blue-violet color, identified today as a variety of zircon (the orange-yellow variety) or sometimes as sapphire (the blue variety). Anciently associated with the hyacinth flower's deep color.

In Scripture, the eleventh foundation of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20); the color of the demonic horsemen's breastplates in the sixth trumpet vision (Rev 9:17); related by name to the hyacinth flower.
scriptures: Revelation 21:20
The tenth, a chrysoprasus; the eleventh, a jacinth; the twelfth, an amethyst.
Revelation 9:17
And thus I saw the horses in the vision, and them that sat on them, having breastplates of fire, and of jacinth, and brimstone.
Exodus 28:28
And they shall bind the breastplate by the rings thereof unto the rings of the ephod with a lace of blue, that it may be above the curious girdle of the ephod.
Numbers 15:38

Speak unto the children of Israel, and bid them that they make them fringes in the borders of their garments throughout their generations, and that they put upon the fringe of the borders a ribband of blue.
corruption_summary: Jacinth is corrupted when the canonical bookending — same word in Rev 9:17 (demonic horsemen) and Rev 21:20 (city foundation) — is missed, blunting the biblical reversal of colors of judgment becoming colors of glory.
corruption_paragraphs: Color-as-coincidence reading. The Greek huakinthos appears in Revelation in two opposite contexts: the breastplates of judgment-horsemen (9:17) and the foundation of the eternal city (21:20). Modernist commentary often treats this as coincidence — the same color is used because it's a natural color for stones AND for breastplates. But Revelation is a deeply patterned book; the SAME word in opposite contexts is the Spirit's deliberate juxtaposition. Judgment colors and city colors meet at jacinth — and the color of fearful trumpet-judgments becomes the color of the eternal city's penultimate foundation.

Blue-thread severance. The OT priestly garments use BLUE pervasively — the lace fastening the breastplate (Exod 28:28), the robe (28:31), the cord on the high priest's mitre (28:37), the borders of every Israelite's garment (Num 15:38). Blue is the priestly color, the color of heavenly origin in the OT typology. To strip the OT blue thread from the eleventh foundation of the city is to lose the priestly-eschatological connection: the blue we once wore around our garments now FOUNDS the city in which we reign as kings and priests (Rev 5:10).
roots_summary: Greek huakinthos (G5191/G5192) — a deep blue-violet stone; eleventh foundation of the New Jerusalem.
roots_lines: Greek huakinthos (G5191/G5192) — jacinth; both a flower (hyacinth) and a precious stone of deep blue-violet color
Eleventh foundation stone of New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20); appears also at Rev 9:17 as a breastplate color of judgment horsemen
Likely modern equivalent: a variety of zircon or sapphire; the deep blue or blue-violet variety
Blue is the OT priestly color (Exod 28:28, 31, 37; Num 15:38) — heavenly origin and priestly identity in cloth
usage: The eleventh foundation is jacinth — the blue that once threaded the priest's garments now founds the city of priest-kings.
The same color that armored the demonic horsemen of trumpet six now beds the city of God: the colors of judgment are reclaimed into the colors of glory.
Blue in Scripture is heavenly; jacinth lays heaven into the eternal city's eleventh course.

etymology: Greek amethystos (G271), Hebrew achlamah (H306) — a purple-violet quartz; the twelfth and final foundation of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20). The Greek name literally means "not drunken" (alpha-privative + methyō, to be drunk) — from the ancient belief that the stone prevented intoxication.
biblical_def: Amethyst is the twelfth and final foundation stone of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20), the ninth stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:19; 39:12), and one of the precious stones in the catalog of Eden's covering stones (in some textual traditions of Ezek 28:13). The Greek name amethystos means "not drunken" — alpha-privative (not) + methyō (to be drunk) — from the ancient pagan belief that wearing the stone or drinking from an amethyst cup would prevent drunkenness. The Bible never assigns the stone any such property, but the lexical history matters: AMETHYST IS THE STONE WHOSE NAME MEANS SOBRIETY, and it is the LAST stone of the city's foundation. The city of God is founded — at its twelfth and final course — on sobriety. Twelve is the biblical number of God's covenant people (twelve tribes, twelve apostles, twelve foundations, twelve gates, twelve pearls). The twelfth foundation completes what the eleventh began: jacinth (blue, heaven, priestly origin) is finished by amethyst (purple, royal and priestly together — the color was rare and reserved for kings, Mark 15:17; Acts 16:14). The city ends as it begins: with kings and priests reigning, all heavenly in origin, sober in their joy, ruling forever. The Babylonian Whore is found drunk on the blood of saints (Rev 17:6, 18:3); the New Jerusalem is founded on the stone whose name means SOBER. The contrast is total. Babel's intoxication versus the city of God's clear-headed worship.
webster_summary: A purple-violet quartz; the twelfth and final foundation of the New Jerusalem and the stone whose name means "not drunken."
webster_full: AMETHYST, noun. A purple or violet variety of quartz, anciently believed to prevent intoxication. The Greek amethystos means literally "not drunken" (a-, not + methyō, to be drunk).

In Scripture, the twelfth and final foundation of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20); the ninth stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:19); possibly among Eden's covering stones (Ezek 28:13 in some textual traditions).
scriptures: Revelation 21:20
The eleventh, a jacinth; the twelfth, an amethyst.
Exodus 28:19
And the third row a ligure, an agate, and an amethyst.
Revelation 17:6
And I saw the woman drunken with the blood of the saints, and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus.
Ephesians 5:18
And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit.
corruption_summary: Amethyst is corrupted when the lexical meaning ("not drunken") is stripped from the city-foundation context, missing the deliberate contrast between Babylon's intoxication and the New Jerusalem's sobriety.
corruption_paragraphs: Lexical severance. The Greek amethystos means literally "not drunken." Of all twelve stones, this one carries the most explicitly meaningful name. Yet most commentaries treat it as just another stone in the catalog, missing the Spirit's deliberate joke: the city of God is FOUNDED, at its TWELFTH and FINAL course, on the stone whose name means SOBRIETY. The contrast with the Babylonian Whore drunk on the blood of saints (Rev 17:6) and the merchants drunk on her luxury (Rev 18:3) is canonical: Babylon is intoxicated; Jerusalem is sober. The twelfth foundation testifies.

Pagan-property co-opting. Modern crystal-healing assigns amethyst all manner of properties ("helps you stay sober," "opens the third eye," "connects to spiritual realms"). The Bible nowhere ascribes any of this to the stone itself. The amethyst is part of the divinely-ordered foundation of the eternal city; it has no independent spiritual power. If you struggle with sobriety, look to Ephesians 5:18 — "be filled with the Spirit" is the New Testament's alternative to intoxication, not the wearing of an amethyst.
roots_summary: Greek amethystos (G271), Hebrew achlamah (H306) — a purple-violet quartz; literally "not drunken"; twelfth foundation of the New Jerusalem.
roots_lines: Greek amethystos (G271) — amethyst; from a- (not) + methyō (to be drunk), literally "not drunken"
Hebrew achlamah (H306) — amethyst; ninth stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:19)
Twelfth and final foundation of New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20) — the stone whose name preaches sobriety completes the city's foundation
Deliberate canonical contrast: Babylon is drunk (Rev 17:6, 18:3) but New Jerusalem is founded on "not-drunken"
usage: The twelfth foundation is amethyst — the stone whose name means SOBER, finishing the foundation of the city that Babylon's drunkenness cannot touch.
Babel founded on intoxication; New Jerusalem founded on sobriety — the contrast runs to the twelfth stone of the eternal wall.
If you want spiritual fullness without intoxication, the Spirit's filling of Ephesians 5:18 is the gospel substitute the gem itself only pictured.

etymology: Hebrew bareketh (H1304) or ekdach (H688) — a glowing red precious stone, likely garnet or red beryl, traditionally translated "carbuncle" in older English from Latin carbunculus ("little coal"), referring to the stone's appearance like a glowing ember.
biblical_def: Carbuncle is one of the precious stones on the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:17; 39:10), one of the stones covering the anointed cherub in Eden (Ezek 28:13), and one of the symbolic stones with which the new Jerusalem will be rebuilt according to Isaiah's eschatological vision: "I will lay thy stones with fair colours, and lay thy foundations with sapphires. And I will make thy windows of agates, and thy gates of carbuncles, and all thy borders of pleasant stones" (Isa 54:11-12). The Latin carbunculus means "little coal" — the stone glows red as if it carried fire within. The third stone of the high priest's breastplate (Reuben-Simeon-Levi row), it represented one of the founding tribes of Israel; in Hebrew, identified probably with red beryl or with garnet, the deep crimson-orange-red gem. The eschatological promise of Isaiah 54 — that God will build Jerusalem's gates of carbuncle — is gloriously fulfilled in Revelation 21:21 where the twelve gates of the New Jerusalem are each a single pearl. The substance has shifted but the principle holds: God beautifies His city's gates with precious things. The gates of the eternal city glow because the Lamb is its lamp (Rev 21:23) — and what once was carbuncle by Isaiah's prophecy is now pearl by John's vision, but in both cases the gates of the city of God are lit from within.
webster_summary: A glowing red precious stone (likely garnet); a stone of the high priest's breastplate, of Eden's covering, and of the prophesied gates of Jerusalem.
webster_full: CARBUNCLE, noun. A precious stone of deep red color, glowing as if with internal fire. The name comes from Latin carbunculus, "little coal." Identified today as garnet (most likely pyrope or almandine) or red beryl.

In Scripture, the third stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:17); a stone covering the anointed cherub in Eden (Ezek 28:13); the material of the gates of Jerusalem in Isaiah's eschatological vision (Isa 54:12).
scriptures: Exodus 28:17
And thou shalt set in it settings of stones, even four rows of stones: the first row shall be a sardius, a topaz, and a carbuncle: this shall be the first row.
Isaiah 54:11-12

O thou afflicted, tossed with tempest, and not comforted, behold, I will lay thy stones with fair colours, and lay thy foundations with sapphires. And I will make thy windows of agates, and thy gates of carbuncles, and all thy borders of pleasant stones.
Ezekiel 28:13

Thou hast been in Eden the garden of God; every precious stone was thy covering, the sardius, topaz, and the diamond, the beryl, the onyx, and the jasper, the sapphire, the emerald, and the carbuncle, and gold.
Revelation 21:21
And the twelve gates were twelve pearls; every several gate was of one pearl.
corruption_summary: Carbuncle is corrupted when the Isaiah 54 promise of carbuncle gates is severed from the Revelation 21 fulfillment of pearl gates — missing the canonical pattern of God beautifying His city's gates with precious things.
corruption_paragraphs: Discontinuity reading. Some dispensational readings hold that Isaiah 54's carbuncle gates and Revelation 21's pearl gates describe entirely different cities (literal earthly millennium Jerusalem vs. eternal New Jerusalem). This atomizes the text. Read together, the canonical pattern is plain: God beautifies the gates of HIS city with precious materials — carbuncle in OT prophecy, pearl in NT vision. Whether you read the gates as literal jewels or as symbol of the glory God bestows on the way INTO His city, the unity of the canonical witness is unmistakable.

Stone-identification fixation. Modern translations debate whether bareketh is carbuncle, emerald, beryl, or chrysolite (different versions render it differently). This is a real scholarly question, but it should not distract from the theological point: the third stone of the high priest's breastplate represented one of the founding tribes of Israel; the stones of Eden covered the anointed cherub before his fall; the same God who chose these stones for breastplate and for Eden is the God who lays foundations and gates of His eternal city. Identity matters less than ordered place in the canonical witness.
roots_summary: Hebrew bareketh (H1304) or ekdach (H688), Latin carbunculus (little coal) — a glowing red stone, likely garnet or red beryl.
roots_lines: Hebrew bareketh (H1304) — "flashing-stone"; third stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:17)
Hebrew ekdach (H688) — translated carbuncle in Isaiah 54:12 (gates of Jerusalem)
Latin carbunculus — "little coal"; describes the stone's deep red glow as if carrying internal fire
Likely modern equivalent: pyrope or almandine garnet, or red beryl; the deep crimson-red translucent variety
usage: The third stone of the breastplate is carbuncle — the priest carried a coal-of-fire over his heart as he entered the holy place.
Isaiah promised gates of carbuncle for Jerusalem; John saw gates of pearl. The substance shifted but the glory held: God's city gates burn with precious light.
Carbuncle covered the cherub in Eden — and now adorns the priesthood that approaches God.

etymology: Hebrew leshem (H3958) — a precious stone identified uncertainly today as zircon, jacinth, or amber-colored opal; the seventh stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:19; 39:12), heading the third row.
biblical_def: Ligure is mentioned only in Exodus 28:19 and 39:12 as the seventh stone of the high priest's breastplate, heading the third row (ligure-agate-amethyst). The Hebrew leshem is one of the most uncertain identifications in the biblical gem catalog — older English translations follow the Vulgate's ligurius; modern translations variously render it jacinth, zircon, amber, opal, or hyacinth. Whatever the exact stone, ligure stood for the tribe of Dan in most traditional reconstructions of the breastplate-tribe correspondence — a tribe with a complicated biblical legacy (associated with judgment, with idolatry of the Danites in Judges 18, with the omission of Dan from the list of sealed tribes in Revelation 7:5-8). Yet ligure stands FIRST in the third row of the breastplate, carried over the high priest's heart as he entered the holy place. The lesson: even Israel's most troubled tribes were borne before God by the priestly mediator. The ligure stone preaches that the people of God are not a meritocracy of perfect performance; they are a body borne by the High Priest who knew their failures and carried them anyway. This typology reaches its fulfillment in Christ, our High Priest who bears even the names of those whose tribal record is mixed (Heb 4:14-16; 7:25). Aaron carried a complicated tribe over his heart on a stone whose very identification has been lost — and yet God knew which tribe, which stone, which name. Christ does the same.
webster_summary: A precious stone of uncertain identification (perhaps jacinth or zircon); the seventh stone of the high priest's breastplate.
webster_full: LIGURE, noun. A precious stone mentioned only in Exodus 28:19 and 39:12 as one of the stones of the high priest's breastplate. Identification is uncertain — variously rendered as jacinth, zircon, amber-colored opal, or hyacinth in modern versions.
Heads the third row of the breastplate (ligure, agate, amethyst), and represents in traditional reconstructions the tribe of Dan.
scriptures: Exodus 28:19
And the third row a ligure, an agate, and an amethyst.
Exodus 39:12
And the third row, a ligure, an agate, and an amethyst.
Hebrews 4:14-15

Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession. For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.
Hebrews 7:25
Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them.
corruption_summary: Ligure is corrupted when the breastplate's tribal-representation function is dismissed as ancient ceremonialism rather than as typology fulfilled in Christ's high-priestly intercession for ALL His people, including the most troubled.
corruption_paragraphs: Ceremonialism dismissal. Modernist commentary often treats the priestly garments and their stones as ancient ritual machinery with no continuing theological weight. But the writer of Hebrews 4-10 takes the entire priestly system as a deliberate shadow of Christ's high-priestly work. The stones — including ligure, whose identification we have lost — represented the tribes carried before God; Christ now carries His people before the Father. To strip the OT priestly system of its typological weight is to lose the gospel logic of the Letter to the Hebrews.

Identification anxiety. Some commentaries devote so much energy to fighting about whether ligure is jacinth or zircon or amber that they miss the central point: God knew exactly which stone He commanded for the seventh position, and Aaron carried it. The IDENTITY of the stone matters less to the typology than the FACT of its inclusion. Christ bears the names of His people whose records are mixed, whose tribes are complicated, whose stones are uncertain; nothing escapes His intercession.
roots_summary: Hebrew leshem (H3958), Latin ligurius (Vulgate) — a precious stone of uncertain identification; the seventh stone of the high priest's breastplate.
roots_lines: Hebrew leshem (H3958) — ligure; appears only at Exod 28:19 and 39:12, with no other canonical use
Latin ligurius (Vulgate translation) — kept in older English versions; modern translations vary
Likely modern equivalent: jacinth, zircon, amber, or amber-opal — the identification has been lost
Seventh stone of the high priest's breastplate; in traditional reconstructions represents the tribe of Dan
usage: Ligure is the stone whose name we have lost — and Aaron carried it anyway over his heart, before God.
Even the troubled tribe of Dan was borne on the breastplate of the high priest; Christ does no less for His people today.
When you cannot remember the stone, remember the Priest who knew it and carried it for you.

etymology: Hebrew shebo (H7618) — a banded variety of chalcedony quartz with concentric color rings; the eighth stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:19; 39:12), middle of the third row. Also appears in Isaiah 54:12 as the material of Jerusalem's eschatological windows.
biblical_def: Agate is the eighth stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:19; 39:12), the middle stone of the third row (ligure-agate-amethyst), and the material God promises for the windows of restored Jerusalem in Isaiah's eschatological vision: "I will make thy windows of agates, and thy gates of carbuncles" (Isa 54:12). Agate is a banded form of chalcedony quartz with distinctive concentric color rings — striped patterns of brown, white, red, yellow, gray that form naturally as the silica deposits over time. Each agate is unique; no two agates have identical banding. This makes the stone a fitting picture of God's particularity: just as no two agates are alike, no two of the believers represented on the breastplate are alike, no two windows in the city of God let in light identically. The eighth stone in the breastplate represents Naphtali in many traditional reconstructions — a tribe whose blessing in Genesis 49:21 was "Naphtali is a hind let loose: he giveth goodly words." The agate's banded variety pictures the speech of a people set free to speak goodly words — variegated speech, particular to each speaker, each ring of color a distinct gift in the chorus. In Isaiah 54 the agate becomes the WINDOW material — the way LIGHT enters the city. Christ is the light of the world (John 8:12), and the city of God has no need of sun or moon because the Lamb is its lamp (Rev 21:23); but in the eschatological vision the light enters THROUGH the agates — through each particular saint's distinct banded testimony, no two alike.
webster_summary: A banded variety of chalcedony quartz; eighth stone of the high priest's breastplate and the material of Jerusalem's eschatological windows.
webster_full: AGATE, noun. A semi-precious stone, a variety of chalcedony quartz formed with concentric or parallel bands of various colors (brown, white, red, yellow, gray, etc.). Each specimen has unique banding; no two are alike.
In Scripture, the eighth stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:19); the material of the windows of restored Jerusalem in Isaiah's eschatological promise (Isa 54:12).
scriptures: Exodus 28:19
And the third row a ligure, an agate, and an amethyst.
Isaiah 54:12
And I will make thy windows of agates, and thy gates of carbuncles, and all thy borders of pleasant stones.
Genesis 49:21
Naphtali is a hind let loose: he giveth goodly words.
John 8:12
Then spake Jesus again unto them, saying, I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.
corruption_summary: Agate is corrupted when its unique-banding property is missed as a picture of God's particularity in dealing with each saint, or when the Isaiah 54 window-promise is read flatly as ancient hyperbole rather than as the eschatological pattern of light entering the city through particular saints.
corruption_paragraphs: Generic-stone reading. Most commentaries treat agate as just one more name in the breastplate catalog. But the stone's defining feature is its UNIQUE BANDING — no two agates show the same pattern. This is theological. Each member of the people of God is a unique work of grace; no two believers' stories form identical bands of providence; no two agate-saints let in the light of Christ identically. To miss this is to flatten the canonical chorus to a monotone.

Eschatology-blind exegesis. Isaiah 54 promises a restored Jerusalem whose windows are agates and gates are carbuncles. Some readings dismiss this as poetic flourish; others insist on literal jewel-windows in a future earthly Jerusalem. The middle path receives the imagery as the Spirit gives it: God will beautify His city's windows with the unique banded stones, the material that admits light through varied particularity. Whether the windows are literal agates or figurative saints, the point holds: light enters the city of God through specific, named, banded means.
roots_summary: Hebrew shebo (H7618) — a banded variety of chalcedony quartz; eighth stone of the high priest's breastplate.
roots_lines: Hebrew shebo (H7618) — agate; eighth stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:19), middle of the third row
A banded form of chalcedony quartz with unique concentric color rings — no two agates show the same banding
Material of Jerusalem's eschatological windows in Isaiah 54:12 — the way light enters the restored city
In traditional breastplate-tribe reconstructions, represents Naphtali (whose Genesis 49:21 blessing was "goodly words")
usage: Each agate is unique in its banding — and so each saint borne on the high priest's breastplate is unique in the work of grace.
God promised windows of agate to His city — the light of Christ enters through particular, named, distinct lives.
The eighth stone of the breastplate is a banded testimony: no two saints' stories are identical, but all together they bear the names of God's tribes.

etymology: Hebrew yahalom (H3095) or shamir (H8068) — a precious stone of extreme hardness, identified today as diamond or alternatively as corundum or hard quartz; the sixth stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:18; 39:11). The Hebrew shamir also describes a substance harder than flint with which God engraves the heart-tablet of Judah's sin (Jer 17:1).
biblical_def: Diamond is the sixth stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:18; 39:11), one of the precious stones covering the anointed cherub in Eden (Ezek 28:13), and — most strikingly — the substance God uses to describe the engraving of Judah's sin: "The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, and with the point of a diamond: it is graven upon the table of their heart, and upon the horns of your altars" (Jer 17:1). The Hebrew yahalom means literally "the smiter" or "the strikingly hard one" — from a root meaning to strike or hammer; the related shamir means "thorn" or "adamant" and is used three times as the harder-than-flint engraving substance (Jer 17:1; Ezek 3:9; Zech 7:12). The stone's defining feature in Scripture is its HARDNESS — its ability to inscribe or be inscribed only at great cost. Sin engraved with a diamond pen is sin engraved permanently; God's word engraved on hearts of stone (Ezek 3:9; 11:19; 36:26; Zech 7:12) is permanent in the opposite direction. The same hardness that makes the stone the perfect engraving tool for sin (Jer 17:1) becomes the perfect material of the new heart God promises His people (Ezek 36:26 — though there the heart is FLESH replacing stone, the inverse picture). The sixth stone of the breastplate, representing Issachar in many traditional reconstructions, sat in the middle row carrying that hardness over the high priest's heart — a daily reminder that what is engraved on hearts (whether sin or righteousness) is engraved permanently. In Christ, the diamond engraving of Judah's sin is overwritten by the diamond engraving of the law of God on the new heart (2 Cor 3:3; Heb 8:10).
webster_summary: A precious stone of extreme hardness; sixth stone of the high priest's breastplate and the substance with which God engraves sin and law on the heart.
webster_full: DIAMOND, noun. A precious stone, the hardest of all natural substances; biblical "diamond" may refer to actual diamond or to corundum (sapphire/ruby) or to other very hard stones. The defining biblical feature is hardness, especially for engraving.

In Scripture, the sixth stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:18); one of Eden's covering stones (Ezek 28:13); the substance with which Judah's sin is engraved on the heart (Jer 17:1); described elsewhere as "adamant" harder than flint (Ezek 3:9; Zech 7:12).
scriptures: Exodus 28:18
And the second row shall be an emerald, a sapphire, and a diamond.
Jeremiah 17:1
The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, and with the point of a diamond: it is graven upon the table of their heart, and upon the horns of your altars.
Ezekiel 36:26
A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.
2 Corinthians 3:3

Forasmuch as ye are manifestly declared to be the epistle of Christ ministered by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart.
corruption_summary: Diamond is corrupted when its biblical engraving-function is reduced to mere preciousness (modern jewelry industry), or when the heart-engraving theology of Jeremiah 17 and 2 Corinthians 3 is severed from the breastplate-stone catalog.
corruption_paragraphs: Jewelry-industry reduction. The De Beers "a diamond is forever" advertising campaign of the twentieth century permanently lodged the diamond in Western consciousness as a luxury love-token. The biblical diamond is something far more weighty: the engraving substance with which God writes sin (and, by promise, His law) on the human heart. "A diamond is forever" is true in a far more frightening way than the ad implied — sin engraved with a diamond pen is sin engraved permanently, until the One who writes a new covenant law on a new heart removes it.

Heart-theology severance. Jeremiah 17:1 says Judah's sin is diamond-engraved on the heart. Ezekiel 36:26 promises a new heart of flesh in place of the heart of stone. 2 Corinthians 3:3 says believers are now "the epistle of Christ" written with the Spirit of the living God on the fleshly tables of the heart. The whole arc — diamond-engraved sin → stony heart removed → fleshly heart inscribed by Spirit — is the gospel in heart-engraving terms. The sixth stone of the breastplate sat over the high priest's heart as a daily testimony: hearts can only be engraved permanently, but the priest's intercession is for those whose engraving needs replacing.
roots_summary: Hebrew yahalom (H3095) or shamir (H8068) — a precious stone of extreme hardness; the sixth stone of the high priest's breastplate.
roots_lines: Hebrew yahalom (H3095) — diamond; literally "the smiter" or "the strikingly hard one"; sixth stone of the breastplate
Hebrew shamir (H8068) — adamant/diamond; the engraving substance harder than flint (Jer 17:1; Ezek 3:9; Zech 7:12)
Defining biblical feature is HARDNESS — used for permanent engraving, whether of sin (Jer 17:1) or covenant law (Heb 8:10)
In traditional breastplate-tribe reconstructions, represents Issachar in the middle row
usage: Sin engraved with a diamond pen lasts forever — and only the Author of a new covenant can engrave a new heart in its place.
The sixth stone of the breastplate was diamond — the priest carried daily over his heart the substance of permanent inscription.
Christ engraves His law on hearts of flesh; the old diamond-cut testimony of sin is replaced by the diamond-permanence of grace.

etymology: Hebrew peninim (H6443) — traditionally translated "rubies" in older English versions, though the Hebrew likely refers to coral, pearls, or red corals rather than the corundum-gem ruby of modern jewelry. Used in Scripture as the benchmark of human-valuable preciousness against which wisdom, the virtuous woman, and the price of a soul are measured (and exceeded).
biblical_def: Ruby (Hebrew peninim) appears in Scripture as the BENCHMARK of preciousness against which higher things are measured — and always EXCEEDED. "The price of wisdom is above rubies" (Job 28:18). "She [wisdom] is more precious than rubies" (Prov 3:15). "For wisdom is better than rubies; and all the things that may be desired are not to be compared to it" (Prov 8:11). "My fruit is better than gold, yea, than fine gold; and my revenue than choice silver" (Prov 8:19). "For the merchandise of it is better than the merchandise of silver, and the gain thereof than fine gold" (Prov 3:14). And in Proverbs 31, the climactic biblical portrait of feminine virtue: "Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies" (Prov 31:10). The Hebrew peninim may not refer to corundum-ruby specifically — many scholars hold it means red coral, or pearls, or the deep-red stones available in the ancient Near East. But the canonical function is consistent: peninim is what people PAY MOST for, and Scripture uses it always to introduce something WORTH MORE — wisdom, the godly wife, the price of a soul. The economic theology is clear: the world esteems certain things as supremely precious; God then names a category of greater preciousness BEYOND what the world prizes. To know wisdom is to recognize what is truly above rubies; to find a virtuous wife is to receive what cannot be bought even with the world's most precious commodity. Christ Himself is the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:30) — the unpurchasable above-rubies treasure that God gives freely to those who ask in faith.
webster_summary: A precious red stone (Hebrew probably coral, pearls, or red corals rather than corundum ruby); the biblical benchmark of preciousness against which wisdom, virtue, and the soul are weighed and exceeded.
webster_full: RUBY, noun. A precious red stone, in modern jewelry the red variety of corundum. The Hebrew peninim, traditionally translated rubies in older English versions, may refer to red coral, pearls, or other deep-red precious materials of the ancient Near East.
In Scripture, used always as the benchmark of preciousness against which higher things (wisdom, the virtuous woman, the soul) are measured and exceeded: Job 28:18; Prov 3:15; 8:11; 20:15; 31:10.
scriptures: Proverbs 31:10
Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies.
Proverbs 8:11
For wisdom is better than rubies; and all the things that may be desired are not to be compared to it.
No mention shall be made of coral, or of pearls: for the price of wisdom is above rubies.
Proverbs 3:15
She is more precious than rubies: and all the things thou canst desire are not to be compared unto her.
corruption_summary: Ruby is corrupted when modern translations remove the consistent "above rubies" rhetoric (replacing rubies with pearls or coral in ways that lose the canonical chorus), or when the Proverbs 31 "price above rubies" is sentimentalized as flattery rather than as serious economic theology about the actual worth of a godly wife.
corruption_paragraphs: Translation-chorus loss. The Hebrew peninim ALWAYS introduces a comparison: this thing is ABOVE the highest-priced commodity. When modern translations swap "rubies" for "pearls" or "coral" or "jewels" in different passages, the reader misses that ONE consistent word is being used as the benchmark across Job, Proverbs, and other wisdom texts. Whether or not modern crystallography matches peninim to ruby specifically, the canonical pattern of consistent comparison is what matters.

Sentimental Proverbs 31. "Her price is far above rubies" is sometimes Mother's Day-flattened into mere romantic flattery for wives. But the text is serious economic theology: a godly wife is OBJECTIVELY MORE VALUABLE than the world's most precious commodity. The Hebrew peninim in Job 28 stood as the highest-priced thing humans could buy; Proverbs 31 says a virtuous woman exceeds even that. This is not a poetic compliment; it is a price valuation. Husbands who treat their wives as accessories or burdens have failed to count what they actually possess. Daughters considering future husbands have a metric: am I being sought as a far-above-rubies treasure or as a possession to be priced down?
roots_summary: Hebrew peninim (H6443) — traditionally rubies; likely red coral, pearls, or red stones; the biblical benchmark of preciousness.
roots_lines: Hebrew peninim (H6443) — rubies; traditionally rendered "rubies" in older English (KJV), though Hebrew may mean red coral, pearls, or red stones
Used in Scripture always as the benchmark of preciousness against which higher things are measured and EXCEEDED
Canonical chorus: wisdom > rubies (Job 28:18; Prov 3:15; 8:11); virtuous wife > rubies (Prov 31:10)
The world's most-priced commodity is the floor, not the ceiling, of God's economy of preciousness
usage: Her price is far above rubies — the virtuous wife is the canonical above-the-benchmark treasure.
Wisdom is more precious than rubies — the Bible names what the world prizes most, only to point past it to what God prizes more.
If you have a godly wife, you possess what cannot be priced; if you have wisdom, you possess what cannot be bought.

etymology: Greek margaritēs (G3135), Hebrew gabish or peninim (H6443) — a precious organic gem formed within the shell of certain mollusks; uniquely in Scripture, the twelve gates of the New Jerusalem are EACH "of one pearl" (Rev 21:21), and the kingdom of heaven is compared to a merchant seeking a pearl of great price (Matt 13:45-46).
biblical_def: Pearl is one of the most theologically loaded gems in the New Testament. Christ used it twice: once in the parable of the pearl of great price (Matt 13:45-46) — the merchant who, finding one pearl of great price, sold all that he had and bought it, an icon of the disciple who counts the kingdom worth everything else combined; and once in the warning not to "cast your pearls before swine" (Matt 7:6) — a sober reminder that the holy things of God should not be flung before those who will only trample and tear. In Revelation, the New Jerusalem's twelve gates are each "of one pearl" (Rev 21:21) — a stunning detail, because pearls in nature are formed when an irritant (a grain of sand, a parasite) enters the oyster's shell and the oyster covers it with layer upon layer of nacre over years of suffering. The gates of the eternal city are the WOUNDED GATES — each formed by the response to an irritant, each the product of long suffering. This is the gospel built into the architecture of heaven: you enter the city of God only through gates formed by suffering — and the supreme suffering is that of the Lamb whose wounds purchased the city. The twelve gates also carry the names of the twelve tribes of Israel (Rev 21:12) — the people of God whose history of suffering and slow accretion of glory mirrors the pearl's formation. Pearl is the only ORGANIC gem in the biblical catalog (every other foundation stone is mineral); the city's gates are the LIVING produce of long covenant patience, and the entrance to glory is always through wounds borne by God Himself.
webster_summary: An organic gem formed within mollusk shells; the parable of the kingdom's surpassing worth, and the material of the twelve gates of the New Jerusalem.
webster_full: PEARL, noun. A smooth, rounded, white or pale-colored gem formed within the shell of certain mollusks (especially oysters) by layers of nacre (mother-of-pearl) deposited over years around an irritant.

In Scripture, the parable of the pearl of great price (Matt 13:45-46); the warning not to cast pearls before swine (Matt 7:6); the material of the twelve gates of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:21), each of "one pearl." The only organic substance in the biblical foundation-stone catalog.
scriptures: Matthew 13:45-46
Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls: Who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it.
Revelation 21:21
And the twelve gates were twelve pearls; every several gate was of one pearl: and the street of the city was pure gold, as it were transparent glass.
Matthew 7:6
Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.
1 Timothy 2:9
In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array.
corruption_summary: Pearl is corrupted when the wound-formation symbolism is missed (treating the city's pearl gates as mere ornament rather than as suffering transfigured) or when the pearl of great price is read sentimentally instead of as the radical kingdom-cost theology Christ intended.
corruption_paragraphs: Wound-formation missed. The detail in Revelation 21:21 — that each of the twelve gates is ONE pearl — is staggering when you consider how pearls form. An oyster covers an irritant with layers of nacre over years; the larger the pearl, the longer the suffering. The gates of the city of God are produced through patient endurance of wound. This is gospel architecture: the entrance to the eternal city is through gates that bear in their very substance the long story of suffering transfigured into beauty. Christ's wounds purchased the city; the saints' wounds patterned the gates. To strip this is to strip the city of its suffering-formed glory.

Sentimental pearl-of-great-price. The parable of the merchant who sells all to buy one pearl is sometimes treated as a touching story about Jesus' love for sinners (Jesus is the merchant; we are the pearl). This inversion misses Christ's intended meaning: the kingdom IS the pearl; the disciple IS the merchant; and the disciple's response should be radical liquidation of everything else to obtain it. The kingdom costs you everything; it is worth everything. Soft-pedaling this empties the parable of its discipleship demand.
roots_summary: Greek margaritēs (G3135) — pearl; an organic gem formed within mollusk shells. The only organic substance in the biblical foundation-stone catalog.
roots_lines: Greek margaritēs (G3135) — pearl; the gem of the kingdom-cost parable (Matt 13:45-46) and the gates of New Jerusalem (Rev 21:21)
Formed naturally by oysters covering an irritant with layers of nacre over years — wound transformed into beauty
Each of the twelve gates of New Jerusalem is ONE pearl (Rev 21:21) — wound-formation as gospel architecture
The only organic substance among the city's foundation gems; every other stone is mineral, but the gates are LIVING
usage: The merchant sold all to buy one pearl of great price — the kingdom of God costs everything, and is worth everything.
Each gate of the eternal city is one pearl — wounds transfigured into glory, suffering layered into the entrance of heaven.
Do not cast your pearls before swine — the holy treasures of God are not for mockery.

etymology: Hebrew pinnah (H6438) — corner; the principal stone at the junction of two walls of a building. In its theological development the most important stone in Scripture: rejected by builders (Ps 118:22), made the head of the corner (Ps 118:22 / Matt 21:42), the chief cornerstone of the church (Eph 2:20), and either a stumbling stone or a sanctuary (1 Pet 2:6-8) depending on faith.
biblical_def: Cornerstone in biblical theology is THE most important stone in Scripture — the stone the builders rejected, which the LORD made the head of the corner (Ps 118:22-23). Christ Himself applied this verse to His own rejection and resurrection: "Did ye never read in the scriptures, The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner: this is the Lord's doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes?" (Matt 21:42). Paul builds the doctrine in Ephesians 2:20 — the church is "built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone" — and Peter develops the two-sided application in 1 Peter 2:6-8: "Unto you therefore which believe he is precious: but unto them which be disobedient, the stone which the builders disallowed, the same is made the head of the corner, And a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence, even to them which stumble at the word." The cornerstone is the stone that DETERMINES THE ALIGNMENT of every other stone in the building. Get the cornerstone wrong, and every wall thereafter is out of plumb. The pre-incarnate Christ chose the cornerstone position before time; the historical Christ revealed Himself in that position to a generation that rejected Him; the resurrected Christ now exalts that position over every architecture of human religion. Either you build on Him and align with what God Himself has set, or you reject Him and stumble at Him; there is no third option. The whole gospel is a cornerstone gospel. The whole of Christian discipleship is alignment with what God has chosen to set first.
webster_summary: The principal stone at the junction of two walls of a building; in biblical theology, Christ Himself as the rejected-but-exalted stone that determines the alignment of God's whole house.
webster_full: CORNERSTONE, noun. The principal stone at the corner of a building, which determines the alignment of the two walls that meet at it. Anciently the cornerstone was the first stone laid, and the most carefully chosen, because the entire building's plumb depended on it.

In biblical theology, the chief cornerstone is Christ Himself (Ps 118:22; Matt 21:42; Eph 2:20; 1 Pet 2:6-8): rejected by Israel's builders, exalted by God, the foundation alignment for the whole household of faith. Either a sanctuary (to believers) or a stone of stumbling (to the disobedient).
scriptures: The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner. This is the LORD's doing; it is marvellous in our eyes.
Matthew 21:42
Did ye never read in the scriptures, The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner: this is the Lord's doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes?
Ephesians 2:20
And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone.
1 Peter 2:6-8

Wherefore also it is contained in the scripture, Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner stone, elect, precious: and he that believeth on him shall not be confounded. Unto you therefore which believe he is precious: but unto them which be disobedient, the stone which the builders disallowed, the same is made the head of the corner, And a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence.
corruption_summary: Cornerstone is corrupted when Christ's exclusive cornerstone-position is replaced (Mary as co-mediatrix in popular Marian piety, the Church magisterium as co-determinant of doctrine in Rome, the pope as Vicar-of-Christ rather than vicar-of-himself, or modern "many cornerstones" pluralism) or when Peter's two-sided application (sanctuary OR stumbling-stone) is softened into universalist generality.
corruption_paragraphs: Cornerstone-displacement Christology. The Roman Catholic system has placed Peter (and his successors) functionally in the cornerstone position — "Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church" (Matt 16:18) — interpreted to mean the papal office is the rock. But Peter himself, when writing his epistle (1 Pet 2:6), points to CHRIST as the cornerstone and to ALL believers as living stones. There is one cornerstone, one chief Shepherd, one Mediator (1 Tim 2:5). Any system that places anyone or anything else in the cornerstone position displaces Christ and produces a building out of plumb.

Universalism softening. 1 Peter 2:8 is a hard verse: Christ is a stone of stumbling "even to them which stumble at the word, being disobedient: whereunto also they were appointed." Modern liberal theology, allergic to the two-sided application, softens this to a universalist "Christ is precious to everyone eventually." But the text is explicit: to believers He is precious; to the disobedient He is a stumbling stone. The cornerstone of God's house judges what aligns with it and what does not. To strip the two-sided application is to lose both the warning to rebels and the comfort to the elect.
roots_summary: Hebrew pinnah (H6438) — corner; the principal stone that determines the alignment of the entire building. The most important stone in Scripture.
roots_lines: Hebrew pinnah (H6438) — corner; the principal stone at the junction of two walls, the first stone laid
Christ Himself is the chief cornerstone (Matt 21:42; Eph 2:20; 1 Pet 2:6) — rejected by builders, exalted by God
Two-sided application: precious sanctuary to believers (1 Pet 2:7), stumbling-stone of judgment to the disobedient (1 Pet 2:8)
The cornerstone DETERMINES alignment; get the cornerstone wrong and every wall is out of plumb; Christ alone occupies this position
usage: The stone the builders rejected is the head of the corner — and that one rejected stone determines the alignment of the whole church.
Christ alone is the chief cornerstone; replace Him with pope, magisterium, Mary, or culture, and your building is out of plumb forever.
Either Christ is precious to you and aligns your life, or He is a stumbling stone you fall over; there is no third option.

etymology: Hebrew zahab (H2091), Greek chrysos (G5557) — the precious metal, in Scripture pervasively associated with the tabernacle/temple, the kingship of God and the Messiah, the heavenly city, and the testing of faith. The most-mentioned metal in the Bible; appears over 400 times.
biblical_def: Gold is the most theologically loaded metal in the entire biblical canon — appearing over 400 times and functioning as the visible language of God's holiness, kingship, and glory. The tabernacle in the wilderness was overlaid with pure gold inside (Exod 25); the ark of the covenant was gold-covered inside and out (Exod 25:11); the mercy-seat was beaten work of one piece of pure gold (Exod 25:17); the cherubim above the mercy-seat were of one piece of pure gold (Exod 25:18); the lampstand-menorah was a single talent of pure gold (Exod 25:39); the table of shewbread was gold-overlaid (Exod 25:24); the altar of incense was gold-overlaid (Exod 30:3); and the high priest's garments were woven with gold thread (Exod 28:5-6). Solomon's temple multiplied this gold-coverage: the inside of the holy place was overlaid with pure gold (1 Kings 6:21), the holy of holies entirely gold (6:20), even the floor (6:30). The wise men brought gold as one of three gifts to the infant Christ (Matt 2:11) — kingly tribute to the King of kings. In the New Jerusalem, the entire city is "pure gold, like unto clear glass" (Rev 21:18, 21) — and the street of the city is pure gold (21:21). And faith itself is described as "much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire" (1 Pet 1:7); the testing of faith refines a treasure greater than refined gold. Gold's biblical theology is consistent: gold is the metal of GOD'S HOLY PRESENCE — wherever God dwells, gold marks the place. The progression from tabernacle gold (small, portable) to temple gold (large, settled) to the New Jerusalem (entire city gold) traces the increasing scope of God's dwelling with man. The eternal city's gold is not decoration but theology made architecture: God Himself dwells there, and what surrounds Him is what has always surrounded Him — pure gold.
webster_summary: The precious yellow metal of God's holy presence; pervades tabernacle, temple, kingly tribute to Christ, the testing of faith, and the entire material of the New Jerusalem.
webster_full: GOLD, noun. A dense, lustrous yellow metal, prized for its incorruptibility, malleability, and beauty. In Scripture, the most theologically loaded metal — appears over 400 times.

In Scripture, the overlay of the tabernacle and ark (Exod 25); the material of the mercy-seat, cherubim, lampstand-menorah, table of shewbread, altar of incense, and high priestly garments; the overlay of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6); one of the three magi gifts (Matt 2:11); the entire material of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:18, 21); the benchmark to which faith is compared and exceeds (1 Pet 1:7).
scriptures: Exodus 25:11
And thou shalt overlay it with pure gold, within and without shalt thou overlay it, and shalt make upon it a crown of gold round about.
Revelation 21:18
And the building of the wall of it was of jasper: and the city was pure gold, like unto clear glass.
1 Peter 1:7
That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ.
Matthew 2:11
And when they were come into the house, they saw the young child with Mary his mother, and fell down, and worshipped him: and they presented unto him gifts; gold, and frankincense, and myrrh.
corruption_summary: Gold is corrupted when the prosperity gospel teaches God's blessing = personal gold accumulation (twisting Deut 8 and ignoring Christ's warnings against trusting riches), or when the Catholic system has accumulated golden ornaments to a degree Christ Himself drove merchants from the temple over, or when modern asceticism strips gold's biblical theology entirely and treats it as inherently corrupting.
corruption_paragraphs: Prosperity-gospel distortion. Modern prosperity teaching often uses Deut 8:18 ("the LORD thy God: for it is he that giveth thee power to get wealth") to suggest God's blessing on the believer is measured in personal gold accumulation. But the same passage warns immediately that Israel will perish if they forget God in their wealth (Deut 8:19). Gold in Scripture is the metal of God's PRESENCE, not the metal of God's REWARD to His favorites; the gold-overlaid tabernacle was Israel's place of worship, not Israel's personal possession. The prosperity gospel reads gold backwards.

Asceticism-overcorrection. Some traditions react to gold-as-luxury by treating ALL gold as worldly and corrupting — refusing wedding bands, refusing decoration in worship spaces, etc. But the God who commanded the gold-overlaid tabernacle and gold-covered ark is not an enemy of gold. The eternal city is GOLD. The question is never "does gold exist?" but "where does gold belong?" Gold belongs in the presence of God (tabernacle, temple, eternal city); gold becomes idolatry when it occupies the place that should be God's (the golden calf, the rich young ruler's possessions, the merchants of Babylon, Rev 18). Asceticism that refuses gold is reacting against an idolatry it has not properly named.
roots_summary: Hebrew zahab (H2091), Greek chrysos (G5557) — the precious yellow metal; appears 400+ times in Scripture as the visible language of God's holy presence.
roots_lines: Hebrew zahab (H2091) — gold; the most-mentioned metal in Hebrew Scripture, especially in tabernacle/temple contexts
Greek chrysos (G5557) — gold; root of chrysolite (gold-stone) and chrysoprasus (gold-leek) of the New Jerusalem foundations
Pervades tabernacle (Exod 25), temple (1 Kings 6), and the entire eternal city (Rev 21:18, 21)
Always associated with the presence of God: where God dwells, gold marks the place; pure gold is the metal of holy presence
usage: Gold is the metal of God's presence — from tabernacle to temple to the entire material of the New Jerusalem.
Faith refined through trial is much more precious than gold tried with fire — God prizes what no mine produces.
The wise men brought gold to the infant King; the redeemed will walk on gold in the city of the King forever.
